transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-22 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~78 mins | Recording: yes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood SE), Priya (Head ML, Aetheris), Marco (Platform Eng), Ellen (Security), Jon (SRE)
Links shared: redwood/benchmarks/soak-templates.xlsx; security pack: redwood.com/security/vpc-checklist (short link)

00:00 Ava: okay everybody, thanks for joining, um we kicked off the invite — is this time still good?
00:08 Priya: yes this works, thanks, excited — we got your pre-read. We mostly want to understand cost tradeoffs for a hybrid setup we described, low tail latency for interactive chat and episodic long context for retrieval augmented flows.
00:22 Samir: perfect, we'll walk through runtime knobs and then jump into the MoE routing economics and rope scaling notes. We'll also propose a soak run on your VPC since you asked for on-prem numbers.
00:35 Marco: quick ask — our infra is on prem VMs with 2xA100 equivalent, and we run Kubernetes with strict node eviction. Preemption is a concern.
00:45 Lena: got it. We'll note preemption constraints; Redwood Private has an eviction-safe mode and we also do lightweight checkpointing of KV cache.
00:55 Ellen: from security, we need to confirm KMS integration and audit logs for token handling and PII filters. Also SSO SAML, RBAC.
01:05 Ava: yes we'll include our security pack. Okay Samir, you wanna start with routing?

01:12 Samir: sure. So at a high level, adaptive routing means we can route requests to a dense Llama/Mistral or to MoE variants depending on the input and cost policy. For Aetheris use-case — short interactive queries should favor a small dense model to keep latency low; long retrieval responses can go to MoE to save compute on conditioning, but the gating overhead matters.
01:32 Priya: quick clar — when you say gating overhead, do you mean extra tokens that the router consumes or the compute to run the gate?
01:38 Samir: both. There's the inference cost of the routing network per token and then the increased memory movement if multiple experts are touched. In practice, cost = base_token_cost + routing_cost + expert_activation_cost where expert_activation_cost depends on number of experts and their sizes.
01:55 Marco: can you quantify that with an example? like when's MoE cheaper than dense?
01:58 Samir: yes. For a 7B dense baseline vs an MoE 8k-expert equivalent, if your average token activates 1.3 experts and your router is ~0.05x the base compute, MoE becomes cheaper after ~C tokens of context or when throughput amortizes the gating. We ran a spreadsheet for similar traffic — we'll send it.
02:20 Priya: that spreadsheet would help. Our traffic is spiky, 1.5k qps bursts for short bursts, with long tail for analytics. We need predictable tail latency at 99.9.
02:32 Jon: yeah, 99.9 is critical, we can't have MoE fallbacks that induce 200ms penalties above baseline.
02:38 Samir: right. That's where adaptive fallback policies help — route by latency SLO. If the router sees queue depth rising, we route to a dense replica or lower-expert-count variant.
02:50 Marco: are those lower-expert variants pre-warmed? we don't want cold starts.
02:55 Lena: you can pin a small pool of dense replicas to be hot, and a scaled pool for MoE. We also do KV cache continuity so long conversations don't need to rebuild state.
03:06 Ellen: about KV cache — we need to know data residency and encryption at rest.
03:10 Ava: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS. KV shards are stored in encrypted disks and audit logs are kept visible to your team. We'll include the KMS integration doc in the pack.

03:22 Samir: shifting to ROPE/positional scaling — Aetheris has long context retrieval, you might want to linearly decay positional embeddings or use ROPE rescaling to avoid attention drift. ROPE scaling (decay) can change attention distribution and affects KV cache hit patterns.
03:40 Priya: we've noticed hallucination growing after 8k tokens in our Mistral runs. Is that likely positional drift?
03:46 Samir: possibly. Two levers: 1) rope decay (scale down positional contribution for older tokens) and 2) segmented KV repair — we evict older KV tiers first. Both reduce attention noise but change token-level quality. You'll need small eval sets to detect regressions.
03:59 Priya: do you have recommended decay rates?
04:02 Samir: common starting point is a geometric decay, factor 0.98 per 1k tokens, but depends on task. We'll provide a tuning grid.

04:15 Marco: about KV-shard sizing — you mentioned sharding the KV cache across GPUs. On our infra we only have 2 GPUs per node. How do we avoid cross-node traffic?
04:26 Lena: one approach is affinity-based routing — route requests whose KV state hashes to local shards to the node. For multi-node, we also support remote fetch with prefetching heuristics to reduce synchronous cross-node waits. That reduces tail latency but increases background traffic.
04:42 Jon: prefetcing introduces bandwidth spikes; with our network we have 25Gb/s — is that sufficient?
04:48 Samir: depends on your hit rates. If you have high locality (80% local), prefetch is light. If hit rates low, you'll pay more network egress. We'll run a soak with your network profile.

05:05 Priya: on quantization, we've been conservative: int8 for everything. Would int4 be safe for Mistral or Qwen?
05:12 Samir: int4 can give big cost savings but quality varies. Mistral often tolerates int4 with per-layer calibration and outlier-aware dynamic ranges; Qwen sometimes needs hybrid int8 for attention layers. We recommend per-model profile testing: 1) baseline int8, 2) int4 for feed-forward with preserved attention in int8, 3) mixed. We'll attach a matrix.
05:35 Priya: do you do dynamic quant during runtime? like choose profile based on token length?
05:40 Samir: Redwood can switch model variants per-request; so yes, you can route long context to an int8 variant for quality and short ones to int4 for cost, but switching costs are model load times unless both are resident. So warm both if you want fast switch.
05:56 Marco: that warms memory — our nodes are memory-limited. How much extra vram do warm variants cost?
06:02 Lena: cold numbers: a 13B in int8 ~ 24GB, int4 ~ 14GB; differences depend on optimizer and KVC. Warm duplicates mean you'll need sum of VRAM; we can help with model packing to co-reside variants by offloading weights to NVMe that we can stream with small penalty.

06:22 Jon: tail-latency graph please — what should we expect for 99.9 under sustained 1.5k bursts with our two-node setup?
06:28 Samir: depends on batching. If you microbatch aggressively (microbatch=8, latency target 50ms) you keep latency low but throughput suffers. For 1.5k bursts you'll need an autoscaler strategy: keep hot dense pool for front-line, spillover to MoE or queued batchers for background. We'll simulate with your distribution.

06:45 Priya: any specific batching tips for short interactive tokens?
06:49 Samir: continuous batching with small time windows (5-10ms) to capture bursts without adding 100ms. Also use prefix caching aggressively — many queries share warm prefixes after retrieval.
06:59 Marco: prefix caching — how does cache invalidation work with policy changes?
07:03 Lena: we version prefix caches. If you change model or routing policy, we can either flush or keep per-version caches. You can set TTLs per-route.

07:12 Ellen: regarding compliance — you said audit logs for token-level costs. We need logs that don't capture PII. Can Redwood redact before storage?
07:20 Ava: yes, there's a pre-ingest filter pipeline. You can run inline redaction or store raw in your own S3 if needed; we can also provide hashed token-level metrics.
07:30 Ellen: and KMS?
07:32 Ava: supports customer-managed KMS, HSM options on-prem. We'll include the integration steps.

07:38 Samir: circling back to MoE economics, one subtlety: rope scaling and KV eviction interacts with expert activation frequency. If older tokens are decayed, the router may route differently, changing expert hotness and making sharding less balanced — which increases cross-node communication. So tuning rope impacts cost indirectly.
07:58 Priya: that's interesting — so we can't tune these knobs independently.
08:02 Samir: exactly — that's why we recommend a small factorial experiment: vary rope decay, expert activation target, and shard count and measure both loss and p99 latency. We'll provide an experiment harness.
08:15 Marco: can you do that harness in our VPC or do we need test data to send?
08:19 Samir: we can run both: we can run a Redwood-hosted harness using sanitized traces, or we can run the agent in your VPC and push metrics to your Grafana. For SLO-sensitive stuff, running in your VPC provides most fidelity.
08:34 Priya: we prefer in-VPC runs. What's the expected duration to see stable metrics?
08:39 Samir: for steady-state throughput and KV patterns, 24 hours is good; for long-term rope drift effects, 72 hours is safer. Hence we suggested a 24-hour soak first.

08:50 Lena: small note on prefetch heuristics — we use LRU+predictive predictors from access traces. If your workload is retrieval heavy with repeated contexts, prefetch hit rates get good quickly.
09:02 Marco: we'll share a week's worth of anonymized traces. Do you need full tokens or hashed keys?
09:07 Jon: we'll do hashed keys and token lengths.

09:12 Priya: about SLOs — our finance team needs a per-token budget. Can Redwood provide a cost breakdown per-path (dense vs MoE vs fallback)?
09:20 Ava: yes, Redwood Console will break down token-level cost by model variant and by route. We'll also annotate with CPU/GPU time and KV hits/misses. We'll export a per-request line item CSV.
09:32 Priya: and do you support custom cost weights? e.g., we want to prefer model variants that minimize monetary spend not GPU time only.
09:39 Samir: yes routing policies can be cost- or latency-prioritized; you can set CostWeight=0.7, LatencyWeight=0.3 and the router will compute expected utility and pick the model variant.

09:51 Marco: any hard limits on number of variants or rollout complexity? we might test 6 variants per route.
09:58 Lena: we commonly run up to 8 variants per route; the console supports canaries, weighted rollouts, and instant fallback. Complexity grows with variants but is manageable.
10:08 Ellen: last sec: do you provide attestation for on-prem? like a signed artifact that the image matches what Redwood published?
10:14 Ava: we do image signing and reproducible build artifacts; we'll include how to verify images and hashes.

10:21 Samir: to wrap up, immediate plan: 1) Samir and team will deploy the 24-hour soak in Aetheris VPC using the harness and your anonymized traces; 2) we will run KV-shard stress and produce 95/99 graphs; 3) we'll deliver quant matrices and suggested decay grid; 4) Redwood will share security integration docs.
10:40 Priya: sounds good. Any blocker on our side? we'll need to whitelist Redwood IPs for agent, and share credentials for KMS test.
10:48 Ava: we'll share a short checklist.
10:50 Marco: timeline — can we get the soak started by next Monday?
10:53 Samir: yes, if we get the traces and whitelist end of this week.
10:56 Priya: ok we'll aim to send traces by Friday.
11:00 Ava: great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and a calendar invite for the next SLO review.
11:05 Priya: thanks, bye.

Post-call notes (auto): transcript has some mis-hearings around product names and numeric values (e.g., expert counts). Shared artifacts: /redwood/benchmarks/soak-templates.xlsx, security checklist link.

End of transcript.
